item.title: After years of maintaining outdated self-hosted tools, I finally found their replacements
item.itunes:title: After years of maintaining outdated self-hosted tools, I finally found their replacements
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been running self-hosted apps for years, and like most setups, mine didn't stay the same. Some services were installed because they looked interesting, while others simply stuck around because they worked well enough. Eventually, I started noticing that a few of them felt outdated compared with newer options available today.

Newer self-hosted projects often have better interfaces, smoother workflows, and features that match the way I work today. So I decided to rethink some of my older choices and see where a change actually made sense.

Here are the replacements that made the biggest difference for me.

Karakeep

My new home for saved links

I switched from Wallabag to Karakeep because I wanted a simpler way to save and manage the things I find online. Wallabag had been part of my self-hosted setup for a long time, but I wasn't using most of what it offered. Over time, it started feeling like more of a tool I maintained than one I actually enjoyed using.

Karakeep feels much more natural for the way I save things. I can quickly bookmark articles, websites, images, and other useful content without thinking too much about where everything should go. The interface is also cleaner, so finding something I saved earlier doesn't feel like a chore. For me, it's a much better replacement for Wallabag.

Karakeep

Karakeep is an open-source, self-hosted bookmarks manager that allows you to add bookmarks from any platform and categorizes them based on tags.

See at Official Site

TriliumNext

Taking control of my knowledge

Joplin had been my go-to note-taking app for a long time, but eventually I wanted something that gave me more flexibility in how I organized information. That's what led me to TriliumNext.

The biggest difference for me is its hierarchical structure. I can create notebooks and sub-notebooks and keep related information together without relying on tags for everything. This works especially well when I'm dealing with notes for different projects, ideas, and reference material. TriliumNext also makes it easy to reorganize my notes as my needs change. I can move information around and build a structure that makes sense instead of forcing everything into a fixed system.

TriliumNext

TriliumNext is a free, open-source, hierarchical note-taking application designed to build large personal knowledge bases.

See at Github

BentoPDF

My PDFs finally feel easier

Earlier I relied on StirlingPDF for everything around PDFs. Stirling-PDF isn’t that old as a self-hosted service, but I eventually wanted something simpler for everyday PDF tasks. That’s where BentoPDF felt like a better fit for my setup. The biggest difference I noticed was how lightweight and fast it felt. PDF tasks that used to feel a little cumbersome now take less time to complete.

I also prefer BentoPDF's interface. The UI is cleaner and more straightforward, so I can quickly find the tool I need without digging through multiple options. Whether I'm merging files, splitting pages, rotating a document, or making other quick changes, everything feels easy to access. For my workflow, the combination of a lighter application, faster performance, and a better UI made the switch an easy decision. It does what I need and stays out of the way when I'm done.

BentoPDF

BentoPDF provides fast, private, and free PDF tools. It processes files locally in your browser, ensuring privacy as your documents never reach their servers. It requires no account, offers all tools for free, and is built for speed.

See at BentoPDF See at Github
I save $100 every month with these 7 docker containers in my home lab

I stopped paying for various cloud services and replaced them with Docker containers that give me more control, and privacy.

By  Yash Patel

Immich

A smoother way to manage photos

PhotoPrism had been handling my photo library for a while, but Immich quickly felt more suited to how I use my photos today. The biggest reason I moved was the overall experience. Immich feels modern, responsive, and much closer to the photo apps I use on my phone.

Uploading photos is straightforward, and I can browse through my library without feeling like I'm waiting for every screen to load. The mobile app is also a big part of why I like it. I can back up photos from my phone automatically and know they will end up on my own server. PhotoPrism still works well, but Immich feels more actively suited to my everyday photo workflow.

Immich
Key highlights
Self-hosted
iOS compatible
Yes
Android compatible
Yes

Immich is a self-hosted photo and video backup solution.

See at Google Play Store See at Apple App Store See at Immich

Homepage

My services finally live together

My self-hosted setup had grown to include quite a few services, so having a simple dashboard became increasingly useful. Heimdall did the job, but Homepage gives me a cleaner and more flexible way to access everything.

I like being able to put all my frequently used services on one page and organize them the way I want. Instead of remembering different URLs or jumping between browser bookmarks, I can open Homepage and get where I need to go quickly.

The dashboard also gives me useful information about some of the services I'm running, which makes it more than just a collection of shortcuts. I can see what I need at a glance without opening each application separately.

Homepage

Homepage is a modern, open-source, fully static, and highly customizable application dashboard and startpage designed to centralize and monitor self-hosted home lab services.

See at Homepage
5 self-hosted services I use for their fantastic mobile apps

Experience the best of both worlds: control and mobile convenience

By  Yash Patel

My self-hosted stack finally feels right

Replacing these older apps wasn't really about chasing newer software. I wanted my self-hosted setup to feel easier to use, maintain, and fit into my daily routine. These replacements have made that possible without giving up the control I value from self-hosting. I also realized that an app doesn't have to be feature-packed to be useful. Sometimes, a simpler tool is exactly what my setup needs.

item.title: Steam's best power-user tricks are buried so deep most gamers never find them
item.itunes:title: Steam's best power-user tricks are buried so deep most gamers never find them
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using Steam for nearly two decades now. I've watched it evolve from a fairly straightforward PC game store into something that sits at the center of almost everything I do with my gaming PC. It's one of the rare few apps on my PC that have earned startup privileges, and rightly so.

What I didn't know about Steam, however, is that apart from being the most user-friendly launcher and storefront, it's also absurdly packed with some great power-user features, as long as you're looking in the right place. All I needed was a way to sort my library in a more tailor-made fashion, and that led me down a rabbit hole of discovering some genuinely remarkable features I never knew existed in Steam.

Big Picture mode on one screen, normal Steam on another

Steam no longer takes over my primary monitor

Steam's Big Picture mode is fantastic, but only when I'm sitting on the couch with a controller in my hand. When Steam decides that my desk monitor needs the same treatment, it does get irritating, to say the least. I now have it configured so Big Picture mode remains exclusive to my 55-inch 4K TV, while Steam opens normally on my 27-inch 1440p display. That distinction makes far more sense for how I actually use my PC.

The setup for this arrangement turned out to be surprisingly simple, too. All I needed to do was go to Steam and enter Big Picture mode. From there, I headed to Settings > Display. Here, under the Preferred Display setting, I set my TCL TV as the preferred display for Big Picture mode, while leaving my monitor as my normal Steam display.

With the TV connected, Steam boots into Big Picture mode on the big screen, ready for controller-based gaming. While I'm at my desk, it behaves like a normal desktop app on my monitor. This small configuration change is something I never even knew about, and now, I can only wish I'd discovered it sooner.

I let Xbox Mode take over my gaming PC's startup, and it solved the Windows 11 problem I never could

This is how you make a PC feel like a gaming console

4
By  Samarveer Singh

Disable the "friend started playing" notifications

I don't need a live feed of everyone's crashes

Steam's friend notifications are useful, and on the occasional midnight gaming session, it can even feel comforting to know that a friend is online, too. However, when someone decides to install 47 mods, launch the game, crash within 30 seconds, and then repeat the process ten times, it can get exasperating. I don't need to know about every single one of those failed launches, especially when Steam dutifully tells me about each one as if something meaningful has happened.

Turns out, you can turn off these notifications by heading into Steam > Settings > Notifications. Find the "When any friend starts a game" option, and disable it. That's it. Steam will stop showing a notification every time someone launches something, while my friends list and everything else remain intact. It's particularly useful if you have friends who treat launching a heavily modded game as a repeated stress test for their PC instead of an attempt actually to play it.

Dynamic Collections automatically organize my library

My Steam library is much bigger than what's actually installed

Steam's library and my installed games are two very different things, but the client doesn't always make that distinction feel particularly helpful. My library has grown into the triple digits over the years, and manually scrolling through all of those games to find what I can actually play is the kind of busywork I don't want from a game launcher.

Steam's Dynamic Collections feature is what fixes that. If I create a new collection, I can choose to make it dynamic, and Steam lets me define filters for it, such as its local install state, genre, playtime, or other library attributes. Once the filters are set, Steam automatically adds every matching game to that collection. If I install something new that meets the criteria, it will appear there without me having to touch the Dynamic Collection again. Again, this is a small feature that not many users actively know about or use, but it does turn a sprawling Steam library into something that actually feels manageable.

Controller configurations from the Steam community blew me away

Someone has probably already fixed your controller problem

Steam Input is far more powerful than I realized, and the best part is that I don't necessarily have to learn how it all works. For supported controllers, Steam lets me browse complete controller configurations shared by other players, complete with descriptions, playtime stats, and community votes. In fact, Valve even supports configurations that can remap physical controller inputs into keyboard and mouse commands.

To try one, connect your controller, open a game's Properties screen, and select Controller. Click Controller Configurator to see all officially available controller inputs. This is where you can click your current button layout, then select Community layouts tailored to the game and controller you're using. Steam also separates configurations by controller type, so you're not accidentally downloading a layout designed around completely different hardware.

This isn't a feature I'll find myself using frequently, but this is particularly handy for older PC games with awkward controller support, or games where the default layout doesn't feel right. Instead of spending half an hour remapping every button myself, I can borrow the setup someone else has already spent half an hour perfecting.

I never knew about persistent notes in the Steam overlay

The Steam overlay is ridiculously nifty

For years, the Steam overlay has been, for me, just the button I pressed when I wanted to invite a friend to a game. I never had much reason to linger there, so I completely missed that Steam has a surprisingly capable notes editor built right into it. In fact, it even has a web browser that can pull up guides without forcing me to Alt-tab out of the game.

The notes feature is the one that genuinely caught me off guard. While playing Hell Is Us, I found myself physically writing down clues, locations, and other bits of information because the game expects me to remember things like an old-school action-adventure title. Then, it occurred to me that I could open the Steam overlay, create a note, and keep everything there instead.

Even better, those notes can remain visible while I'm playing, effectively turning them into a set of virtual sticky notes. I can keep track of clues, objectives, or anything else I don't want to forget without having my notebook share space with my keyboard on my deskmat.

Steam lets you download games over the local network

An incredible feature for roommates and second-PC owners

For anyone wanting their friend or roommate to hop into a game they like, or even for those with a second PC at home connected to a TV, Steam lets you copy game files from another PC on the same local network. Instead of pulling the game once again from the internet off Steam's servers, this feature can prove particularly useful in places like college dorms, where several people might be downloading the same 100GB game on the same connection.

If sharing a game via a local network with another device, you must ensure that the Steam account receiving the game also has a license for the game, i.e., has purchased it via the Steam store.

If your roommate or friend already has a game installed, Steam can transfer the files directly to your PC, saving bandwidth and potentially dramatically reducing installation time. Valve says that a wired connection can reach around 100 MB/s.

To enable it, go to Steam > Settings > Downloads > Game File Transfer, then choose whether transfers are allowed between your own devices, Steam friends, or anyone on the local network. The PC receiving the game files will automatically check for usable local files before downloading from Steam's servers, meaning there's nothing else to babysit.

Steam has been hiding a lot in plain sight

I've come to particularly appreciate that none of these features have required me to fundamentally change how I use Steam. All they've done is remove little points of friction or add tiny QoL changes to my usual Steam user experience. After spending this long with the platform, I had convinced myself I already knew where everything was, which makes finding something genuinely useful buried behind an unfamiliar menu all the more satisfying.

Steam has become so much more than the storefront it started as, and I suspect I've only scratched the surface. There are probably still settings I haven't opened or shortcuts I haven't pressed, and I can't help but wonder what else I've been missing.

item.title: I ditched Chrome bookmarks for a self-hosted dashboard that automatically deletes dead links
item.itunes:title: I ditched Chrome bookmarks for a self-hosted dashboard that automatically deletes dead links
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have a bad habit of bookmarking every interesting website I come across. Over time, my bookmarks folder has amassed hundreds of links, some of which are from websites that don't even exist anymore. However, as a digital hoarder, deleting these en masse is something I'm just not comfortable with.

Look, keeping track of these links is far from easy. Chrome makes it a cinch to remember a URL, but it does nothing to help me find out if these links are still active. So, when I came across a tool that largely tries to solve that problem, I immediately jumped on it.

NextDash is a self-hosted bookmark dashboard that checks the links I save and gives me tools to manage them. Not just that, the app is a full-fledged bookmark replacement dashboard giving you a much easier way to actually get to your bookmarks.

The health dashboard keeps an eye on bookmarks

Find broken or duplicate links automatically

The biggest reason I installed nextDash is its health dashboard. The entire purpose of the dashboard is to check my bookmarks and identify any issues that crop up. But more than the health check, the way that nextDash handles the check is what makes it brilliant in my books.

Anytime you run a health check in nextDash, it can identify everything from broken links to redirects, duplicate URLs and even issues in the bookmark itself. If you've got a selection of bookmarks that you access regularly, you can just add them to your dashboard for quick access, but the key reason I switch to nextDash is the built-in health check.

Here's how I use it. One of the biggest reasons I save a lot of links is research. I might bookmark a product page, or a Github repository that's shaping up into a good project worth covering here on XDA. Sometimes, I'll bookmark documentation or just an article to catch up with later. Most of the time, these links work out just fine. However, every so often, as it happens, the page might have moved, or the link might have changed. In fact, there have also been instances when I saved the same bookmark twice. It's unnecessary redundancy.

Chrome offers no way to handle any of that. NextDash does.

Moreover, it does that while giving you plenty of control. Not every bookmark needs to be constantly checked. A bookmark link to my local server is going to stay the same. NextDash lets you set different checking modes for individual bookmarks. So, you can turn the built-in health check off for specific bookmarks. Since there's support for background checks, you don't even need the dashboard open for it to run on a schedule.

I'll be honest, some of the data presented by nextDash isn't of too much use to me. I like the fact that I can get uptime history and response-time information, but, personally, it's not a feature I have a lot of use for. However, if you want to monitor a particular website to gauge reliability and uptime, nextDash's health checks could come in handy.

Elsewhere, you can also use nextDash's health view as a clean-up tool. Since it gives you an overview of the links that are no longer working, it's easy enough to delete these from the health view than manually auditing hundreds of bookmarks.

The inbox feature can turn nextDash into a read-it-later app

Like I mentioned earlier, nextDash is a full-fledged dashboard and if you want to use it like that, you certainly can. To that end, one of the most interesting and fairly unique features I've come across in the app is the Inbox.

I'll often save a page because it looks useful. Web pages such as shopping links don't necessarily need a page, category or tag. NextDash gives me an inbox where I can put those links and deal with the organization aspect later. In case it even needs organization. I tend to use this place as my read-it-later list.

The app is plenty extensible with integrations for Raycast, Alfred and even Apple Shortcuts. I'm just scratching the surface of what nextDash can do, but clearly there are a lot of possibilities here.

It's part of what makes nextDash different from other book managers, of which plenty exist. It differentiates itself with a few features that add significant productivity to any workflow.

item.title: Microsoft will roll out a security patch that may negatively impact your gaming performance
item.itunes:title: Microsoft will roll out a security patch that may negatively impact your gaming performance
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Windows 11 enables kernel-level memory integrity by default in October 2026.
  • Memory integrity may lower in-game framerates and hurt gaming performance.
  • Turn off memory integrity in Core Isolation before gaming, then turn it back on after.

Receiving new security measures on Windows is usually good, but those new measures usually need to take up some resources to actually work. If you're someone who pushes their PC to its utmost to get the best framerates, these additions may end up harming your performance a little bit. Next month, Windows is receiving a security update that may harm your in-game framerates, but you can turn it off before it even arrives on your PC.

Windows 11's upcoming security update may harm your framerates

But you can proactively disable it

As reported by The Verge, Windows 11 is receiving a new security update in October. This will be a kernel-level system that should keep your PC safe from malware:

"Beginning in October 2026, Microsoft will expand memory integrity protection across eligible devices, helping you and your organization benefit from stronger kernel-level protection from sophisticated attacks by default with little or no additional configuration. This change reduces security complexity while helping you establish a stronger security baseline across your environment."

Unfortunately, memory integrity can also bite into in-game performance, meaning this new security measure may end up harming your framerate without a clear reason as to why. However, Microsoft does say that, if your PC currently has memory integrity disabled, it will stay disabled even after the update rolls out.

As such, The Verge says that people can enter "Core Isolation" into their Windows 11 Search and disable memory integrity ahead of time. It also notes that Microsoft's advice is to disable it before you game, then re-enable it when you're all done playing for the day. Regardless, if you try gaming next month and you notice a strange drop in framerate that wasn't there the month before, it's worth checking this before doing anything else.

item.title: Wi-Fi 8's real upgrade is that your devices start talking to each other instead of at each other
item.itunes:title: Wi-Fi 8's real upgrade is that your devices start talking to each other instead of at each other
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every generation of Wi-Fi has made significant jumps in terms of maximum throughput, with Wi-Fi 7 bringing us to 46 Gbps (Wi-Fi 6/6E topped out at 9.6 Gbps). This upgrade in speed makes every successive Wi-Fi standard theoretically superior to the previous one, but the average user isn't seeing the benefit on the ground. Most people in the US are still using 300 Mbps connections, not multi-gig plans that can benefit from Wi-Fi 7.

While Wi-Fi standards have improved stability, latency, and range over time, Wi-Fi 8 is the one that's expressly targeting "Ultra High Reliability." It's not about raising theoretical throughput anymore; it's about making Wi-Fi more consistent in a world overflowing with devices vying for the same airwaves.

Wi-Fi 8 will focus on stability instead of speed, but I don't even care about Wi-Fi 7 yet

The core of Wi-Fi is broken and needs a rethink.

Ethernet cables have dedicated twisted pairs for either route, which isn't possible on a wireless medium, at least not on consumer hardware.

This makes Wi-Fi inherently chaotic, since all your devices, plus the neighboring networks, share the same radio waves for transmitting. This arrangement might seem perfect, but each AP is transmitting without really knowing about what the others are up to.

What this means is that two devices, if they're far enough, connected to the same AP, can be completely unaware of each other. Due to the decentralized nature of DCF, devices make transmission decisions independently, leaving room for retransmissions and latency spikes.

item.title: My years-old gaming PC became the best AI machine in the house, and it only needed one upgrade
item.itunes:title: My years-old gaming PC became the best AI machine in the house, and it only needed one upgrade
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My RTX 4070 Ti Super was just as transformative for my gaming experience as it was for local AI inference on my old gaming PC. This rig was built many years ago around an RTX 2070 Super, a Ryzen 5 3600 with 32GB of DDR4, and until this upgrade, served to store the family's documents and whatever local models could fit inside 8GB of VRAM, which is a shorter list than it sounds.

The GPU was the only part that I changed in the build. I didn't drop in a new CPU, a new motherboard, or a new DDR5 kit (especially not in the middle of this DRAM crisis). Despite that, this old PC has become something I route every local AI task to.

The RTX 2070 Super was just enough, but 8GB VRAM put a hard limit

My choice of local models was heavily hardware-limited

Until the swap, 8GB of GDDR6 defined what my PC could do with local AI, and certainly within that limit, it did well. Qwen 3.5 4B at Q4_K_M quantization took up around 3.3 GB of VRAM and generated 80.94 tokens per second at 8K context, which was fast enough for single-file Python scripts to come back within seconds. Gemma 4 E4B at the same quantization ran at 80.60 tokens per second while taking up 3.2 GB of VRAM, and could help me with the summarization and note-making.

The trouble started when I decided to try going one or two steps up in the model hierarchy. Gemma 4 12B at Q4_K_M is about 7.1–7.5GB of weights before the KV cache and compute buffer, and 8GB of GDDR6 meant the model would certainly spill into the system memory, bringing the prompt processing down to an excruciating crawl, making it good for absolutely nothing.

I didn't even bother trying Ministral 3 14B or GPT-OSS-20B on this rig, as I mentally disqualified myself from running these models knowing the hardware I had. The CPU in this case was completely blameless, because once a model left the VRAM, there was absolutely nothing that could make it usably fast. That's one of the reasons why I didn't look into upgrading the chip.

I ditched cloud AI for these 3 local models, and my 8GB GPU handles them all

8GB may not be great for games, but it can be more than enough for these local models

1
By  Abhinav Raj

The 4070 Ti Super doubled the VRAM, and I was spoiled for choice

16GB GDDR6X made me stop doing the math before downloading a model

Nothing else changed in the rig besides the GPU, and nothing else needed to anyway. With 16GB of GDDR6X available at 672 GB/s, the models that previously spilled on my 2070 Super now fit completely on the VRAM with room to spare, provided I set the context where it was ideal for my tasks. I personally like to run these through Ollama for ease of use, though llama.cpp remains the right harness if you're measuring any model's ceiling rather than its everyday behavior. My use case concerns the latter.

GPT-OSS-20b at its native MXFP4 occupies around 12GB, and because it activates only 3.6B of its 21B params per token, it generates at 123 tokens per second at 16K context. Gemma 4 12B at Q4_K_M, on the other hand, uses 7.66GB of weights (8.4GB in total with cache at 32K context), leaving room for the image and audio input that the Unified model handles natively, averaging about 63 tokens per second, which is a comfortable, usable pace.

My Zen 2 chip stays mostly idle through all of this, except, of course, moving the prompt to the GPU. Once the weights and the cache are resident in the VRAM, the rest of the platform barely matters.

More VRAM changed what I was willing to ask my PC

Bigger models handle tasks where 4B models kept second-guessing

I never had any complaints with my 4B models, and I still keep many of them (like Qwen 3.5 4B) around for simple reasoning, summarization, or document analysis tasks. What moving to bigger models essentially changed is the class of task I can trust the model with.

Being able to benefit from a bigger context window on my local models means that I can drop a large model documentation or benchmark data comprising 40–50 pages in context and still be able to rely on the model to not invent details or lose track of the conversation. This is exactly the kind of problem that kept pushing me back to cloud services with the smaller models.

The more, even convenient quality-of-life advantage of having more VRAM resources shows up in my coding workflow. Previously, the Python utilities that took me three or four rounds of nudging on Qwen 3.5 4B can now be finished on the first or second attempt on GPT-OSS-20b using MXFP4 quantization.

By now you'd probably have realized given the direction I'm going in. The very same models I ran on the 2070 Super also feel like different tools with more than enough headroom to breathe.

Gemma 4 E4B can keep its full 128K context loaded without me having to watch over the cache, which makes it hold an entire thread coherently through an entire evening of back-and-forth. And of course, on the occasions when E4B is not enough, its bigger siblings can simply just be downloaded and used alongside it, or instead of it.

Gemma 4 is lightweight, runs on my 16GB laptop, and costs $0 to keep me productive offline

There's no laptop I own that doesn't have it

9
By  Abhinav Raj

VRAM is the new oil in the local AI landscape

The local AI landscape certainly seems to be moving at a breakneck pace right now, so it's important to be honest and say that 16GB is no longer where the ceiling is.

Qwen 3.8 27B just rolled out, Devstral Small 2 requires at least 24GB for quantized setups (and double that for full unquantized FP16), so, suffice it to say that frontier open models are firmly in the "24GB and above" territory. However, it does not mean that doubling the VRAM didn't equip my machine to do a lot more for me and my workflow, because it certainly helped turn my aging PC into a local inference powerhouse, at least for me.

GPT-OSS-20b at its native MXFP4 occupies around 12GB, and because it activates only 3.6B of its 21B params per token, it generates at 123 tokens per second at 16K context. Gemma 4 12B at Q4_K_M, on the other hand, uses 7.66GB of weights (8.4GB in total with cache at 32K context), leaving room for the image and audio input that the Unified model handles natively, averaging about 63 tokens per second, which is a comfortable, usable pace.

My Zen 2 chip stays mostly idle through all of this, except, of course, moving the prompt to the GPU. Once the weights and the cache are resident in the VRAM, the rest of the platform barely matters.

More VRAM changed what I was willing to ask my PC

Bigger models handle tasks where 4B models kept second-guessing

I never had any complaints with my 4B models, and I still keep many of them (like Qwen 3.5 4B) around for simple reasoning, summarization, or document analysis tasks. What moving to bigger models essentially changed is the class of task I can trust the model with.

Being able to benefit from a bigger context window on my local models means that I can drop a large model documentation or benchmark data comprising 40–50 pages in context and still be able to rely on the model to not invent details or lose track of the conversation. This is exactly the kind of problem that kept pushing me back to cloud services with the smaller models.

The more, even convenient quality-of-life advantage of having more VRAM resources shows up in my coding workflow. Previously, the Python utilities that took me three or four rounds of nudging on Qwen 3.5 4B can now be finished on the first or second attempt on GPT-OSS-20b using MXFP4 quantization.

By now you'd probably have realized given the direction I'm going in. The very same models I ran on the 2070 Super also feel like different tools with more than enough headroom to breathe.

Gemma 4 E4B can keep its full 128K context loaded without me having to watch over the cache, which makes it hold an entire thread coherently through an entire evening of back-and-forth. And of course, on the occasions when E4B is not enough, its bigger siblings can simply just be downloaded and used alongside it, or instead of it.

Gemma 4 is lightweight, runs on my 16GB laptop, and costs $0 to keep me productive offline

There's no laptop I own that doesn't have it

9
By  Abhinav Raj

VRAM is the new oil in the local AI landscape

The local AI landscape certainly seems to be moving at a breakneck pace right now, so it's important to be honest and say that 16GB is no longer where the ceiling is.

Qwen 3.8 27B just rolled out, Devstral Small 2 requires at least 24GB for quantized setups (and double that for full unquantized FP16), so, suffice it to say that frontier open models are firmly in the "24GB and above" territory. However, it does not mean that doubling the VRAM didn't equip my machine to do a lot more for me and my workflow, because it certainly helped turn my aging PC into a local inference powerhouse, at least for me.

I’ve tried just about everything to stop my coding agent from making the same mistakes repeatedly. I tried pointing out the mistake in my prompt, explaining exactly what went wrong, and adding another instruction to AGENTS.md. The agent would follow it for that session. The next time I gave it a similar task, it would make the same mistake again.

I then made the model read the file before it started working. So my coding agent now has a record of its previous failures, and it actually uses that record when approaching the same kind of task again.

Coding agents don’t learn from your corrections

Corrections disappear when you restart the session

Correcting a coding agent doesn’t modify the underlying model. The agent is using the model at inference time, so your correction becomes additional context rather than new training. The model can follow the correction while it remains in the conversation, but a new session starts without that context unless the information has been saved and retrieved.

AGENTS.md makes instructions persistent, though it still cannot enforce them. For example, Codex loads the file into the model’s context as a user-role message. The model reads those instructions alongside your prompt and everything it collects while working. A rule in AGENTS.md therefore influences the next action without making the prohibited action impossible.

A coding agent keeps adding source code and command output to its context, which can bury an important project rule. Adding every correction to AGENTS.md eventually creates the same problem. The file becomes another long collection of instructions that the model has to process.

If you use Claude code, you can use hooks to send the agent back to review its output. However, the review remains part of that session. It doesn’t preserve why the failure happened. If you want to prevent the same mistake later, you need to put that lesson back into the model's context before it chooses its approach, which is where MISTAKES.md fits in.

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

19
By  Mahnoor Faisal

MISTAKES.md records what the agent should do differently

It's a project-specific record of failures

MISTAKES.md is a project-specific record of confirmed failures. Each entry explains what the agent did wrong and identifies the decision that caused it. It then gives the agent a specific rule to apply when it encounters the same situation again. I started with this 12-line template:

# MISTAKES.md
Review relevant entries before planning or editing code.
Add an entry after a confirmed mistake or user correction.
Keep entries short, specific, and project-related.
Merge repeated mistakes instead of creating duplicates.
Do not record transient tool failures or unverified guesses.
## Entry format
### [YYYY-MM-DD] [Short title]
**Mistake:** [What the agent did wrong]
**Root cause:** [Why the decision failed]
**Prevention:** [The rule to apply next time]
**Verification:** [How to confirm the mistake was avoided]

The root cause and prevention fields are the most important parts of an entry. Recording that the agent “broke authentication” doesn’t give the next session enough information. The file needs to explain which decision broke it. The prevention rule should then describe the correct approach in terms the agent can apply directly.

I would suggest not adding routine tool failures to this file. For example, a command failing because the network dropped doesn't teach the model anything. The same applies to typos that were fixed immediately. You should also avoid adding generic instructions such as "write clean code" because it's just more text and doesn't change a specific decision.

Make the agent read MISTAKES.md

Before it starts working

MISTAKES.md will only be useful when the agent reads it before making any decisions. I added an instruction to AGENTS.md telling the agent to review the file before planning or editing code. Since I use Claude Code, I import AGENTS.md through CLAUDE.md.

I also use a SessionStart hook to load the file automatically. The hook runs a small script whenever Claude starts a new session or resumes an existing one. That script checks whether MISTAKES.md exists and reads its contents. Claude Code then adds the output to the model’s context before the first prompt. The same hook runs again after the context is compacted, so the entries don’t disappear during a longer task.

For the unaware, hooks are small scripts that run automatically when a coding agent reaches a specific point in its workflow. The trigger could be the start of a session or an attempted tool call. Unlike a prompt instruction, the agent doesn’t decide whether to run a hook. The agent harness executes it whenever the configured event occurs. You will often encounter the term “hooks” in Claude Code, but the feature isn’t exclusive to it. Lifecycle hooks are common across coding-agent harnesses, although their names, triggers, and configuration differ between agents.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

item.title: Paint.NET has finally arrived on Linux, but it is "extremely experimental" for now
item.itunes:title: Paint.NET has finally arrived on Linux, but it is "extremely experimental" for now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Paint.NET runs on Linux, but it's extremely experimental, vibe-coded, and unstable.
  • It requires the portable build, WINE 11.14+, adding a d3dcompiler_47 DLL override, installing DXVK, and running with /wine.
  • It often runs slowly or crashes unpredictably, but it's a start for Paint.NET fans.

One app I really missed when I moved from Windows to Linux was Paint.NET. It filled this amazing niche for tasks that were too complex for regular Paint, but not complex enough for me to justify booting up GIMP. And Linux does have Krita and Pinta, and they're both excellent, but my heart still yearns for Paint.NET.

Well, I have good news and bad news. The good news is that the creator of Paint.NET has released a Linux version of their app. The bad news is...it's still experimental. Like, extremely experimental; ten times worse than you're imagining.

Paint.NET has been released on Linux, albeit in a very unstable state

It'll even run if you're lucky enough

Credit: Rick Brewster

Over on the Paint.NET forums, the creator of the app, Rick Brewster, created a post detailing his efforts to get Paint.NET onto Linux. It uses Wine, and Brewster says the code is mostly vibe-coded, not yet checked, and runs off what he calls a "trust me bro" mentality. But it does run, although it's a little choppy.

Here is the list of requirements Brewster posted for Paint.NET on Linux:

  • Use the portable version of the app. The installer will NOT work.
  • You must be using at least WINE version 11.14. Seriously, just use whatever the latest version is.
  • You need add a registry key so that WINE doesn't try to override a DLL with its own version which does not work. Run this command to do so: (and if someone knows how to make it so that this step isn't needed, please tell me): wine reg add "HKCU\Software\Wine\DllOverrides" /v d3dcompiler_47 /d native /f
  • You should have DXVK installed.
  • You must run the app with the /wine command-line parameter

    Your reward for checking all of these boxes is a version of Paint.NET on Linux that sometimes runs very slowly and sometimes just crashes on you when it feels like it. But hey, it's a start, even if it's mostly vibe code held together with a bunch of string and a healthy dose of hope.

    Wine 11 rewrites how Linux runs Windows games at the kernel level, and the speed gains are massive

    Wine 11 is the biggest jump for Linux gaming in years.

    38
    By  Adam Conway

item.title: I ditched my Raspberry Pi for an old Android phone, and my self-hosted services finally stopped throttling
item.itunes:title: I ditched my Raspberry Pi for an old Android phone, and my self-hosted services finally stopped throttling
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I think of cheap, tiny, and portable hardware for small homelab services, the Raspberry Pi is the first thing that comes to my mind. And if I visit a homelab thread on a tech forum, Pi comes up as a settled recommendation, not something to question again.

But last month, when I deployed a DNS server on my old Android phone, I started thinking otherwise. The experiment proved to me that the phone was capable of running homelab workloads, but the DNS server never really pushed it. That was when I decided to pile the phone with similar workloads to what a Pi typically runs and see which one struggled under more load.

Pi-hole delivered solid results

That said, the setup process was a tad complex

A few weeks ago, I experimented with my old Android phone (POCO F1) for a DNS server. This was a dedicated test to see whether it could replace a Raspberry Pi for something that is supposed to run 24/7. Android phones are not designed for these types of tasks.

A DNS server usually needs free port 53 to bind to, but a consumer-grade Android phone doesn’t give out that option openly. I had to play around with root permissions, Termux, and proot-distro to actually make it work. Port 53 is privileged, so running Pi-hole's DNS service on the phone was more interesting than an ordinary web service. But the result in the end was proof that an old Android phone can act like a proper server.

I turned an old Android phone into a home server, and it’s more useful than my Raspberry Pi

Don't let it collect dust in a drawer.

34
By  Jasmine Mannan

The setup might be complex, but DNS filtering is a light workload for modern hardware like my phone’s SDM845 and 6GB LPDDR4X RAM. That is why these types of services are usually handed over to a single-board computer (SBC) like a Raspberry Pi. Even though the phone was running 24/7 and handling my whole home network, it didn’t break a sweat; there was no noticeable CPU/thermal load.

The F1 experiment gave me the evidence that it could host a service, but it didn’t prove whether it could replace an SBC under a broader homelab workload. Another experiment was necessary to evaluate it. So I did, this time looking for the ceiling instead.

I didn't want an easy second phone. I wanted the weakest one.

I gave it everything a Pi usually carries

The POCO F1 already answered the easy question that an old Android phone can run an always-on service without any issues. But if I were to compare it directly to a Raspberry Pi, say Pi 5, the F1 wasn’t a good candidate. The 2018 F1 had powerful hardware enough to feel ahead of its time, but that’s exactly what made it an unfair comparison with the 2023 Pi 5.

Now, I had a new question: how much do I downgrade the phone to make it an apple-to-apple comparison with the Pi 5? Fortunately, the perfect device was lying in my drawer, the Moto G5 Plus. It was a 2017 phone with a Snapdragon 625, lower than the F1’s Snapdragon 845 but closer to the Pi 5's 2.4 GHz quad-core Cortex-A76. It was already running on a custom ROM and had root privileges, so it was easy for me to set it up as a small Linux machine.

My exact model was XT1686-DS with 4 GB RAM. And even before I started anything, free -h showed me 2.1 GB RAM was already used by Android at idle. Then, I followed the same Pi-hole setup through Termux/proot on the G5 Plus and kept it running. And finally moved to an actual Docker via the same root access. I deployed a few more regular services that I use in my homelab, such as Uptime Kuma, Vaultwarden, and a few more. Why Uptime Kuma and Vaultwarden, specifically? Because they are the best examples of services one should host outside their main homelab to cover the blind spots.

So, by the end, I had something concrete to compare to the Raspberry Pi setup. When the services were up and running, I wasn’t looking for a phone that could keep up. I was waiting for the one most likely to fail.

One throttles quietly. One didn't.

The ceiling that never showed up

The Pi 5 is a smart machine. It could be thermal throttling right now, but you would never know because it never announces it; instead, it quietly manages things behind the scenes, avoiding a crash. When it is under a continuous load, it usually drops clock speed to manage the heat, especially while running without any active cooler, the default setup for a lot of homelab Pis.

You can notice it from slow-loading dashboards, delayed responses for running services such as Pi-hole, and small things that I would usually blame on the SD card. But if you want a certain answer, vcgencmd get_throttled is the way to verify it. If it returns 0x0, that means the board is running fine, and apart from 0x0, if you see anything else, the Pi at some point managed the load to protect itself.

Coming back to the phone. If I keep aside the CPU performance — eight ARM Cortex-A53 cores running up to 2.0 GHz is itself a good number — the memory was the first thing where it started showing a little up and down. As already mentioned, even before starting I only had around 1.4 GB of available memory.

The Pi-hole, Vaultwarden, BentoPDF, and Uptime Kuma containers combined were always under 500 MB. Pi-hole was at around 80–100 MB, Vaultwarden at around 70–90 MB, BentoPDF would range between 20MB and 30 MB, and Uptime Kuma was the heaviest of the others at around 200-250 MB. item.title: Plex paywalled the features I need, so I started using Jellyfin alongside it
item.itunes:title: Plex paywalled the features I need, so I started using Jellyfin alongside it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using Plex ever since the self-hosting media server was first released. However, the company has started to nickel-and-dime users, and now some of its best features are completely paywalled behind Plex Pass.

Since some of the features I like require Plex Pass, I started running Jellyfin alongside Plex with essentially the same media library. Virtually all Plex Pass features are available in Jellyfin without paying a dime.

Plex's walled-off garden of features

You might not notice until you need them

I usually forget what features require a Plex Pass subscription until I want to use them. I find it quite irksome when the platform throws up a screen wanting me to choose a Pass package. It's no secret that you need Plex Pass to access features like hardware-accelerated transcoding and downloads, but even simple functions like skipping intros and credits require a subscription. Plex also changed its remote streaming policy in 2025, making the feature available only to Plex Pass subscribers.

Every self-hosting media server admin should be able to access their personal media from remote locations. However, under the policy change, remote streaming requires a Plex Pass subscription ($7/month, $70/year, $750/lifetime) or a Remote Watch Pass ($2/month, $20/year). The company has moved features to Pass over the years since its initial rollout. It's hard to know what's next. The entire Plex service might become locked down and become subscription-based. So, to get Plex's paywalled features, I turned to Jellyfin.

I stopped choosing between Plex and Jellyfin, and my media server is better because of it

Both Plex and Jellyfin are better when you stop trying to choose between them

19
By  Samarveer Singh

Using Jellyfin for Plex Pass features

An eye-opening experience once I got started

It took me a while to get into the Jellyfin craze and set up my server. I was skeptical that it could handle the paywalled Plex tasks well. Even though there has been dissent among the project's leadership, I still moved my media library to Jellyfin. Overall, however, I've been impressed with how well Jellyfin handles my content.

Everything that's included in Plex Pass is completely free with Jellyfin. Some features require a plugin or manual configuration, like remote streaming or skipping intros or credits. Other functionality, like hardware encoding, SyncPlay (watch parties), HDR-to-SDR tone mapping, and Live TV/DVR with a compatible tuner, is built in.

It's also beneficial that the community is growing, and developers have released improved clients, which are plentiful across all platforms. Some third-party clients work better with the server than others, but in the end, I always find one that does specific tasks well. Plus, I add countless plugins to my Jellyfin server to make it do exactly what I need.

I'm not choosing one platform over the other

I use both Plex and Jellyfin in tandem

Since Jellyfin and Plex can run alongside each other on my network without conflict (that I've experienced yet anyway), I see no reason to choose one over the other. I guess I could pick Jellyfin over Plex on principle alone. It's open source, and everything is free, including a vast array of plugins. Then again, Plex can do certain things better or more easily than Jellyfin, and vice versa.

However, I am ditching Plex Pass, which is likely a first step in breaking away from Plex altogether. The more I get comfortable with how Jellyfin works, get my metadata and library properly configured, and keep trying new plugins, the more I appreciate the self-hosted platform's freedom and flexibility. Sure, paying a monthly or yearly Pass to have features that "just work" without manual configuration saves time, but there's something to be said about putting in the work. It's nice to get the satisfaction of building the perfect self-hosted media system for my media.

Teaming Plex and Jellyfin

A strong media duo

Running both lets me keep the familiar Plex system and user interface, while still switching to Jellyfin when I need functionality that's locked behind a paywall. Plex might look more polished and seem easier to manage, but once I started digging into Jellyfin, I found all sorts of cool things I can do with my media without paying a cent.

Plex is fine for local-only streaming with the occasional GPU-heavy load. I use Plex for its glossy user interface and speed on my Nvidia Shield, since it's built-in and optimized for the device. When a UHD or 4K file needs transcoding for lower bandwidth or other incompatible devices, I use Jellyfin because it includes hardware transcoding.

I also use Jellyfin more on various devices where I want a specific client. For instance, I might use Moonfin for theming on my phone or streaming box, and Streamyfin or Findroid for movies on Android. Jellybox is a free client for my self-hosted streaming music player. I like that it provides most of the features Plexamp includes without paying. Plenty of Jellyfin clients suit specific needs or devices.

6 Jellyfin plugins that add free features Plex charges you for

Jellyfin's plugin ecosystem does what Plex charges for, and it's free

11
By  Samarveer Singh

Running Plex and Jellyfin simultaneously pays off

I appreciate that Jellyfin is open source and does everything that's trapped behind Plex Pass. The community also offers media-consumption customization with a wide variety of plugins and clients. It's difficult to break away from Plex, but I can't justify paying a convenience fee for features I can manually configure myself. So, for now, running both apps in tandem gives me the best of both worlds.
